This is the part I want reviewed hardest, because you are right that the obvious implementation of this test passes against a cockpit that removes the row optimistically — the assertion just has to land in the millisecond before the frame arrives, and on this machine it would.
The hold is not a timer and it is not a branch for tests.
Do not reflow the list a person is clicking on.

Between "revoke pressed" and "the runtime answered", the rows hold still. Otherwise the row under the cursor can move while the cursor is on it, in a surface where a mis-click grants or removes authority. So

blocks.text:
await window.cockpit.pause();          // frame_ack(seq, ready: false)
… await invoke('intent', …) …
await window.cockpit.resume();         // frame_ack(seq, ready: true)

spans.text: honours it, because the delivery valve was already there for backpressure:
Ordering is what makes it deterministic rather than probable.

The pause and the intent are two messages on one bounded queue, drained in order by the one thread that also emits. The pause is therefore in force before the intent is submitted, which is before the world can move. There is no window in which the frame could arrive early.
